tagline.text: A camping lake where a chapel steeple rises from waters dammed by Pinatubo's ash

location.label: Location
location.text: Around Barangay Aglao, San Marcelino, Zambales

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 (transport, boat, camping fees and meals, rough estimate per person for 2 days and 1 night)

children.text: Lake Mapanuepe in San Marcelino, Zambales, formed when lahar blocked a river after the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo. The steeple and cross of the Saint Barbara chapel still rise above the water over a drowned village, and visitors come to camp and take boat rides on the lake.

Lake Mapanuepe is a freshwater lake in the municipality of San Marcelino, Zambales. After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, lahar (volcanic mudflows) poured into the Marella River and blocked the Mapanuepe River, and the dammed water filled the Mapanuepe Valley, creating the lake in 1991–1992. It was made not by nature but by a disaster, which is what sets it apart. The lake sits at the confluence of the Marella and Mapanuepe Rivers, and its water drains out through the Santo Tomas River.
According to Wikipedia, the lake is about
4.1 km
long at most and
2.5 km
wide, covers about 648 hectares and is up to about
deep. Its surface lies at about

above sea level and it holds ten small islets. It did not form in a single lahar event: the debris dam was breached and rebuilt again and again before the lake reached its present size. Its size has varied over time. Wikipedia says that at its fullest the lake covered about 670 hectares and stored about 75 million cubic meters of water, and gives a shoreline of about
33 km

, a figure that is hard to define and best taken as a rough guide. The lake also appeared on an American TV monster-hunting show, after local fishermen reported large dark fish-like creatures that earned the nickname "Pinatubo Monster." It is only a fun story, so take it lightly.

Villages including lower Aglao, Buhawen and Pili were submerged. As a result, only the steeple and a large metal cross of the Saint Barbara chapel remain above the water in the middle of the lake. The chapel served as a small place of worship for residents of Buhawen. If you take a boat close to it, you can see for yourself what remains of a village that lost its home to disaster.

Today the lake is a destination for campers and boat tours. Aeta indigenous communities live around it, and Aeta people work as boatmen, guides and sellers of farm produce. With no electricity and weak mobile signal, it suits anyone who wants to leave the city and spend a night under the stars, but the road is rough and preparation is demanding, so first-time visitors are safer joining a group tour or hiring a local guide. Development plans are also part of the story: reports say a floating solar project on the lake was proposed and preparatory assessments such as water testing were carried out, while Aeta groups raised concerns about consent and land use. Remember that the lake is the home of the Aeta people before it is a tourist site. Conditions change within a year, so check the latest situation locally before you go.

blocks.title: The submerged Saint Barbara chapel steeple

children.text: This is the symbol of the lake. As your bangka approaches the steeple and cross rising from the water, it hits home that a village once lay beneath the lake. It photographs best at sunrise or around sunset.

The village of Aglao, the starting point for the lake, has a viewpoint that also serves as the boat landing for the campsite. It is usual to hire a guide at the village entrance and pay the environmental and entrance fees there.

The campsite is split into four phases. Phase 2 has the best views but is crowded, while Phase 1 is quieter, near the stream and Aeta communities. Phases 3 and 4 are open grassland. Each phase has toilets, showers and small stores, but supplies are brought in, so prices are high.
The lake boat tour is offered for an extra fee and goes close to the steeple. At the stream, designated spots are set aside for water play, where you can safely dip your feet.
ATVs are reported to be available for rent at Phase 3, and gravel biking is also popular. Check fees locally.
The lake area is known for birdwatching, landscape photography, and sunrise and astrophotography. A tip for drone pilots: eagles and falcons may swoop at a drone, so fly with care.
Aeta people sometimes sell bamboo bird-shaped flutes or farm produce at the lake. Talk with them respectfully and buy only what you need. Do not buy animals such as parrots or iguanas.

blocks.title: Ten small islets and lake scenery

children.text: The lake holds ten small islets and is a favorite photo spot. Many people shoot sunrises, sunsets and night skies. When passing between the islets by boat, follow your guide's judgment.

items.title: Overnight camping trip
items.subtitle: From Aglao across the lake to the campsite

children.text: Take a Zambales-bound bus from Manila and get off in San Marcelino. You can also come via Olongapo and continue by jeepney.
Buy food and water at the San Marcelino market. Shops by the lake are few and expensive.
Take a jeepney from the market to Aglao. The jeepney often runs once a day in the morning and returns in the afternoon, so you need a plan B if the timing does not fit.
Drop your bags near the Aglao barangay hall, pay the environmental fee and find a guide.
Cross by bangka from the viewpoint landing to the campsite and pitch your tent.
Watch the sunset. With no electricity it gets very dark after sunset, so bring a lantern.
On day two, catch the sunrise and tour the chapel steeple by boat.
Pack up and carry all your trash out. Head back to the village in time for the afternoon jeepney.
The schedule on this route can easily shift, so confirm your guide and transport plan the day before.

items.title: Day trip
items.subtitle: Viewpoint and boat tour to the steeple

children.text: Leave Manila on the first bus.
Arrive in San Marcelino and check transport to Aglao.
Look over the lake from the Aglao viewpoint and sign up for a boat tour.
Circle the steeple by boat and return to the village.
Head off in time for your bus back to Manila.
A day trip is difficult if the jeepney timing does not work, so confirm in advance with a local contact.
You can take a Zambales-bound bus such as Victory Liner and get off in San Marcelino. One blog gives the fare as about
, but it varies by company and season, so check at the terminal.
You can also take a bus to Olongapo and transfer to a jeepney to San Marcelino.
Jeepneys run from the San Marcelino market to Aglao, but they often go once in the morning and return in the afternoon, and the schedule can change without notice.
Park near the Aglao barangay hall and cross to the campsite in an outrigger bangka from the viewpoint landing.
Off-road vehicles such as 4x4s can drive in, but they have to cross streams and must go with a local guide.
Depending on the stream level, private vehicles may not be able to cross, so avoid the rainy season.
For first-time visitors, a group or private tour is described as the easiest option. Contents and prices differ by operator.

For camping, the dry months of November–May are safest. In the rainy season the stream rises, roads turn muddy and the weather over the lake can change quickly. April and May are strong-sun, sweltering months, so plan to rest in the middle of the day at campsites with almost no shade.
Nights from December to February are relatively cool and good for stargazing. In any season, avoid boating on windy or rainy days.

There are no lodgings by the lake, and camping in your own tent is the norm. Bring a tent, cooking gear, a power bank or generator, lanterns, water and food. Each phase has small stores, but goods are brought in by boat, so prices are high and the selection is limited. A toilet visit is reported to cost about ₱5 and a shower around ₱10, so carry plenty of small change. Phase 2 is said to have paid internet, but do not plan your trip around a stable connection.

Cattle roam the area and may raid food bags, so secure your food and trash at night. It is better to buy your supplies in San Marcelino town before heading in. Ask locally whether anyone sells fish from the lake, and avoid raw or doubtful food.
Electricity and mobile signal are weak, so bring offline maps and a power bank.
Swimming is not recommended because of submerged structures and branches. Use the designated spots or the stream.
Do not buy animals such as parrots or iguanas from Aeta sellers.
Keep noise down late at night and carry out all your trash.
Fly drones with care, as eagles and falcons live here.
Jeepney schedules can change, so confirm them with your guide the day before.
Do not leave valuables in your tent; keep them on you at all times.
If it is your first visit, tell the boatman which camping phase you want in advance. Each phase has a different feel.
To catch the sunrise, agree on a time with the boatman the day before. Keep drones and cameras in a waterproof bag so rain and spray do not soak them.
There were reports of a motor bangka capsizing on the lake in late August 2026, with deaths. Wear a life jacket, keep to the passenger limit and do not board in bad weather.
Do not exceed the boat's passenger limit and check the life jackets. Check the latest safety guidance with the local government.
Tourists have reported thefts of belongings in the past, and police have been deployed. Keep your valuables safe.

There is an abandoned mine on the eastern shore, and mercury contamination was once reported, though the mine side denied it; a 2024 study found heavy metals generally within standard limits, with copper and manganese above limits at some sites, and mercury was not measured separately. Do not drink the lake water.
In the rainy season the stream can swell and make access dangerous.
Respect the land and culture of the Aeta community and ask permission before taking photos.
The volcano whose 1991 eruption created this lake. You can trek to its crater lake.
